_meta.rule: 按 id + 字段关联；值为英文译稿，源文案改动需重新生成

sun.atmosphere: Photosphere: hydrogen 90.97%, helium 8.89% (rest are trace elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon, etc.)

earth.atmosphere: Nitrogen ~78%, Oxygen ~21% (trace amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, etc.)

mars.atmosphere: Carbon dioxide 95.1%, Nitrogen 2.6%, Argon 1.9% (trace amounts of oxygen, carbon monoxide, etc.)

jupiter.atmosphere: Hydrogen 89.8%, Helium 10.2% (trace amounts of methane, ammonia, etc.)

saturn.atmosphere: Hydrogen 96.3%, Helium 3.25% (with trace amounts of methane, ammonia, etc.)

pistol_star.note: [AI Reproduced 2026-10-27: physical/mass_sun, physical/mass_kg set to empty]

antares.note: [AI Reproduced 2026-10-27: physical/mass_sun, physical/mass_kg set to empty]

proxima_centauri.note: 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/orbital_velocity_km_s,orbit/eccentricity】 【2026-11-11 Authority Source Verification: Kervella et al. 2016 gives a=8700(+700/-400) AU、P=547000 yr、e=0.50; the original 13000 AU was the instantaneous linear separation at that time instead of the semi-major axis, and the orbital velocity has been recalculated according to a/P/e】

m87_star.note: Schwarzschild radius ~128 AU, larger than Neptune's orbit; accretion disk jets extend thousands of light-years.

sgr_a_star.note: Schwarzschild radius ~0.085 AU (~12.7 million km); orbital determination by decades-long tracking of surrounding stellar orbits.

ton618.note: Schwarzschild radius ~1300 AU; luminosity ~4×10⁴⁰ W. A 2019 remeasurement yielded a lower mass (~40.7 billion M☉), the classical estimate of 66 billion M☉ is adopted here.

ic1101_bh.note: Literature estimates range 40–100 billion M☉; the median value of 50 billion M☉ is adopted here for order-of-magnitude reference only.

gw190521.note: Formed by the merger of two black holes of 85 M☉ + 66 M☉; approximately 8 M☉ was radiated in the form of gravitational waves; the signal lasted only 0.1 seconds. The distance is luminosity distance (caused by cosmic expansion, larger than comoving distance).

cyg_x1.note: 2021 VLBA precise measurement: 21.2 M☉, 7240 light-years; horizon rotation speed ≥95% the speed of light.

v404_cyg.note: Mass estimate 9~12 M☉, 9 M☉ is adopted here; outburst in June 2015 made it one of the brightest X-ray flares in the preceding 50 years.

m42.note: Diameter approximately 24 light-years; gas cloud mass approximately 2000 M☉, with thousands of stars forming inside.

m1.note: Diameter approx. 11 light-years; supernova remnant from the 1054 CE explosion, hosting a 33-millisecond pulsar at its core.
m1.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Hubble's most detailed image of the Crab Nebula

m16.note: Diameter approx. 70 light-years; the "Pillars of Creation" captured by Hubble in 1995 ranks among the most famous astronomical photographs ever taken.
m16.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · WISE infrared panoramic view of the Eagle Nebula

m20.note: Diameter approx. 40 light-years; three dark dust lanes divide the nebula into three lobes, hence its name.

m8.note: Apparent size 110×50 light-years (elliptical), equivalent diameter approx. 90 light-years; contains open cluster NGC 6530 within.
m8.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · WISE mosaic of the Lagoon Nebula

horsehead.note: Diameter ~3.5 light-years; it does not emit light itself, a dark dust lane in front of the background emission nebula IC 434.

m57.note: Diameter ~2.6 light-years; gaseous shell ejected by a dying star, with a white dwarf visible at the center.
m57.image_credit: NASA/ESA/STScI · Hubble Ring Nebula True Shape

ngc7293.note: Diameter ~5.7 light-years; resembles a giant eye, nearby and large, a representative planetary nebula.
ngc7293.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · GALEX Ultraviolet Eye of God Panorama

m2_9.note: Diameter ~1.4 light-years; interactions within the binary system shape its symmetric two-lobed structure.
m2_9.image_credit: NASA/ESA/STScI · Hubble Bipolar Planetary Nebula M2-9

rosette.note: Diameter ~130 light-years; a 2024 NOIRLab study proposed a closer distance (~2600 light-years) and smaller size (~55 light-years); the classical value is adopted here.

barnards_loop.note: Diameter ~300 light-years; the ionized edge of the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex.

tarantula.note: Diameter ~1000 light-years; if placed at the Milky Way's location, its radiance would be bright enough to cast shadows.

milky_way.note: Diameter ~100,000 light-years (100,000–200,000 light-years for different apertures); the Sun is ~26,000 light-years from the Galactic Center, with an orbital period of ~230 million years.
milky_way.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Artist's concept of Milky Way structure (not a real photograph)

m31.note: Diameter ~220,000 light-years; it will merge with the Milky Way in ~4 billion years.
m31.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · GALEX ultraviolet mosaic of the Andromeda Galaxy

m33.note: Diameter ~61,000 light-years (D25 isophote); distance estimate 2.38~3.07 million light-years, adopted 2.88 million.

lmc.note: Diameter ~14,000 light-years; host galaxy of the Tarantula Nebula.
lmc.image_credit: ESA/NASA/JPL-Caltech · Herschel infrared full view of the Large Magellanic Cloud

smc.note: Diameter approx. 7000 light-years; connected to the Large Magellanic Cloud by a gas bridge.
smc.image_credit: ESA/NASA/JPL-Caltech/CSIRO/NANTEN2 · Small Magellanic Cloud infrared composite (Herschel/Planck/IRAS/COBE)

m87.note: Diameter 12~240,000 light-years, adopt 240,000 light-years; central black hole M87* has a separate entry.
m87.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Spitzer infrared M87 elliptical galaxy (host galaxy of the first imaged black hole)

m104.note: Diameter approx. 50,000 light-years (D25 isophote); the bulge and edge-on dust ring form the "Sombrero" shape.

m51.note: Diameter ~77,000 light-years; distance estimate 23~31 million light-years, adopted 28 million.
m51.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Hubble Space Telescope Whirlpool Galaxy

m81.members: Forms an interacting galaxy pair with M82

m82.note: Diameter ~37,000 light-years; gravitational interaction with M81 triggers intense starburst.
m82.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/SAO/NOAO · M82 visible light + NuSTAR X-ray composite

ngc1300.note: Diameter ~110,000 light-years; central bar structure and outward-extending spiral arms are highly regular.

ic1101.note: A 2024 A&A study measured a diameter of ~1.7 million light-years; values vary greatly with aperture, and the galactic halo may extend to ~6 million light-years. The 1.7 million light-year value is adopted here (radius 850,000).

stephens_quintet.note: The group spans about 350,000 light-years; four galaxies are undergoing merging and tidal disruption (NGC 7320 is merely a foreground galaxy).
stephens_quintet.image_credit: NASA/ESA · Hubble Space Telescope Stephan's Quintet (1999)

m45.note: Diameter of about 14 light-years; age of about 100 million years, young stars are wrapped by a blue reflection nebula.
m45.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Spitzer Infrared Pleiades (Seven Sisters + reflection nebula)

hyades.note: Diameter of about 15 light-years; age of about 625 million years, forming the V-shape of the Taurus head.

m44.note: Diameter of about 16 light-years; age of 6~7 hundred million years, an open cluster barely visible to the naked eye.
m44.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Beehive Cluster (Keck/CFHT observation, two exoplanets marked)

m67.note: Diameter ~20 light-years; age ~4 billion years, more than 100 Sun-like stars.

r136.note: Diameter ~10 light-years; age only 100~200 ten thousand years, containing several giants with a hundred times the mass of the Sun.
r136.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Hubble Panorama of the Large Magellanic Cloud's Tarantula Nebula (starburst region hosting R136 cluster)
r136.members: Contains R136a1, one of the brightest known stars (~215~315 M☉)

m13.note: Diameter ~145 light-years; the first human radio message was transmitted toward it by Arecibo in 1974.

m22.note: diameter about 100 light-years; one of the brightest globular clusters, individual stars can be resolved with binoculars.
m22.members: hundreds of thousands of member stars

omega_cen.note: diameter about 170 light-years; anomalous mass and stellar population, possibly the core of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way.
omega_cen.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · WISE Omega Centauri Globular Cluster

local_group.note: diameter about 10 million light-years; total mass estimated at 2~5×10¹² M☉ (the Milky Way + Andromeda combined is already about 3×10¹² M☉).
local_group.members: more than 80 galaxies (including the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum, Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, etc.)

virgo_cluster.note: Diameter ~15 million light-years; the Local Group is falling toward it under its gravitational pull.

laniakea.note: Diameter ~520 million light-years; defined by Tully et al. in 2014 based on galaxy flow fields, later studies suggest it is not a gravitationally bound structure.

great_attractor.note: Region scale ~400 million light-years; lies behind the Zone of Avoidance, discovered via galaxy peculiar velocities. Centered near the Norma Cluster (ACO 3627); its mass composition remains debated.

hercules_corona_wall.note: Diameter ~10 billion light-years (comoving scale; size remains debated); discovered in 2013 based on gamma-ray burst distribution.

cmb.note: Comoving distance ~45.7 billion light-years; temperature 2.725 K, fluctuations only ~10⁻⁵, these fluctuations are the seeds of all present-day galaxy structures.

observable_universe.note: Radius ~46.5 billion light-years (comoving distance); age ~13.8 billion years; ordinary matter 4.9%, dark matter 26.8%, dark energy 68.3%.
observable_universe.image_credit: ESA/NASA · Planck satellite and Cosmic Microwave Background (artistic concept)

m17.note: A large star-forming region in the direction of Sagittarius, containing open cluster NGC 6618; it appears swan/horseshoe-shaped in visible light.
m17.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · Spitzer Infrared Swan Nebula M17

m27.note: Gas shell ejected by a dying star with a central white dwarf; the first planetary nebula in the Messier catalog.

ngc3372.note: The equivalent diameter varies (approx. 260~460 light-years, depending on whether outer dark nebula structures are included); it contains Eta Carinae, the Keyhole Nebula and multiple massive star clusters.
ngc3372.image_credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/STScI · Webb Telescope Carina Nebula "Cosmic Cliffs"

ngc7000.note: It belongs to the same giant H II region as the Pelican Nebula (IC 5070), separated into two parts by dust lanes.
ngc7000.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Caltech/IPAC · North America Nebula (visible + infrared composite)

m101.note: In 2011, Hubble assembled 51 images to produce its largest and sharpest spiral panorama to date.
m101.image_credit: NASA/STScI/JPL-Caltech/Chandra · Multi-wavelength composite of Pinwheel Galaxy M101

m64.note: Also known as the Sleeping Beauty Galaxy; gas in its outer disk rotates in the opposite direction, thought to be a remnant of an ancient galaxy merger.
m64.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Hubble Black Eye Galaxy M64

m83.note: 6 supernova outbursts have been observed, a frequent target for amateur and professional observers.
m83.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech · GALEX ultraviolet Southern Pinwheel Galaxy M83

ngc5128.note: One of the closest radio galaxies (radio source Cen A); the central supermassive black hole jet extends thousands of light-years.

ngc4038.note: The effective radius includes two tidal tails (the two cores of NGC 4038 and NGC 4039 are about 25,000 light-years apart); the merger-triggered starburst has formed tens of thousands of star clusters.

m11.note: One of the open clusters with the largest known membership; a bright cluster in the Scutum Star Cloud.
m11.image_credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UMD · Wild Duck Cluster M11 captured by Deep Impact

m7.note: A small number of deep-sky objects recorded by ancient people naked-eye, a large clump of starlight visible to the naked eye.

ngc4755.note: Age of only about 7 million years; a small colourful cluster near Crux, visible with binoculars by naked eye.

gw150514.subtype: Binary black hole merger (gravitational wave event)
gw150514.note: Initial state: 36 M☉ + 29 M☉ binary black holes, approximately 62 M☉ after merger, about 3 M☉ of mass released in the form of gravitational waves; distance estimated from the luminosity distance at redshift z≈0.09.
gw150514.image_credit: NASA/CXC · Schematic of gravitational waves from binary black hole merger

eta_carinae.note: Mass (approx. 100~150 M☉), radius (approx. 60~800 R☉) and temperature changed drastically during the 1843 'Great Eruption' false supernova, a single value cannot be given, hence null; surrounded by the Homunculus Nebula ejected by itself.
eta_carinae.image_credit: NASA/STScI · Eta Carinae and the Homunculus Nebula, Hubble WFPC2

vesta.note: The second largest body in the asteroid belt, a differentiated protoplanet (iron core + rocky mantle + crust); parent body of HED meteorites; Rheasilvia impact crater in the Antarctic region has a diameter of about 500 km, and the central peak on the crater floor is about 20 km high. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/temp_k; Fill:distance_ly,orbit/obliquity_deg】

halley.note: Nucleus is peanut-shaped, approximately 15×8×8 km; retrograde orbit (inclination 162°); perihelion speed can reach 54.6 km/s; its 1986 apparition was imaged up close by the Giotto spacecraft, next apparition is July 2061.
halley.image_credit: Nucleus of Comet Halley photographed by ESA/NASA Giotto in 1986

sirius_b.note: Dense remnant with mass comparable to the Sun and radius of only about 5634 km (smaller than Earth), surface gravity roughly 400,000 times that of Earth; it is the first member in the Sirius system to exhaust fuel and evolve, while the bright companion Sirius A remains a main-sequence star. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/inclination_deg,orbit/eccentricity】

eridani_40a.note: Also named Keid, it forms a triple system with white dwarf B and red dwarf C; the B/C binary takes about 8000 years to orbit it; it is well-known for appearing in Star Trek canon as the sun of the Vulcans. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

eridani_40b.note: It appears faint yet 'white', which implies an extremely small volume — this observational reasoning laid the foundation for white dwarf physics; it also orbits together with a red dwarf (40 Eridani C). 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/eccentricity】

crab_pulsar.note: Neutron star left by the supernova explosion in 1054; rotation period 33.39 ms; diameter only ~20 km, surface temperature ~1.6×10⁶ K, a bright synchrotron radiation source across all wavebands (radio to gamma-ray). 【AI Review 2026-10-27 (Only 1 submission succeeded): Clear:physical/temp_k; Fill:physical/lum_sun,orbit/rotation_period_hours】

vela_pulsar.note: Located at the center of the Vela Supernova Remnant, rotation period 89.33 ms; famous for periodic 'glitches' (sudden spin-up), a natural laboratory for probing superfluid structures inside neutron stars. 【AI Review 2026-10-27 (Only 1 submission succeeded): Clear:physical/radius_sun,physical/radius_km; Fill:physical/temp_k,physical/lum_sun,orbit/rotation_period_hours】

sgr_1806_20.note: Magnetar with the strongest magnetic field in the universe (~10¹⁵ G), rotation period 7.5 s; its giant flare on 27 December 2004 released more energy in 0.1 s than the Sun emits in 250,000 years — it would be lethal if occurring much closer. Mass not directly measured (typical neutron star value ~1.4 M☉), hence left blank.

alphacen_a.note: G2V star with nearly identical spectrum and mass to the Sun; forms a close binary with Alpha Centauri B (orbital period ~80 yr), while Proxima Centauri orbits this bright pair at ~0.2 ly away.

alphacen_b.note: Slightly smaller and fainter orange dwarf companion; combined apparent magnitude -0.27, the third-brightest 'star' in the sky (listed as fourth in a few references).

castor.subtype: White main-sequence star (A1Vm sextuple star system)
castor.note: One vertex of the Winter Triangle. Appears as a single star to the naked eye, but it is a multiple system of six stars: pairs A and B are each spectroscopic binaries, plus a distant red dwarf companion pair (YY Geminorum).

pollux.note: The brightest star in Gemini (brighter than its 'brother' Pollux, despite a later Bayer designation). Its exoplanet Thestias (β Geminorum b) was confirmed in 2006, with a mass of approximately 2.3 Jupiter masses and an orbital period of about 590 days. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Empty:physical/lum_sun】

capella.note: The fifth-brightest star in the northern sky. The primary pair consists of two yellow giants (orbiting each other in roughly 104 days), with two additional faint red dwarf companions.

aldebaran.note: The brightest star in Taurus; its radius has expanded to about 44 times that of the Sun. It lies along the line of sight to the Hyades cluster but is a much closer foreground star and not a member of the cluster. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

spica.note: The two blue-white stars orbit each other in only about 4 days; strong tidal forces distort them into egg shapes (ellipsoidal variable). It forms the Spring Triangle with Denebola and Arcturus. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/inclination_deg,orbit/eccentricity】

regulus.note: Nearly aligned with the ecliptic, it is frequently occulted by the Moon and planets. Its rotation period of about 15.9 hours distorts it into a noticeably oblate spheroid; the surface gravity at the poles is roughly twice that at the equator.

formalhaut.note: A bright star isolated in the southern sky (no other bright stars within 20°). Its debris disk was among the first debris disks imaged directly by telescopes, and the nature of the candidate planet Fomalhaut b within the disk remains controversial.

altair.note: One vertex of the Summer Triangle. Its rotation period of about 7.77 hours distorts it into an oblate spheroid (equatorial radius roughly 25% larger than polar radius), a deformation confirmed directly by interferometry; the folklore that it faces Vega across the Milky Way is widely known. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Clear:physical/radius_sun,physical/radius_km】

deneb.note: Luminous at roughly 200,000 times the Sun's luminosity, it is one of the brightest known A-type supergiants; its estimated distance of 1400~2600 light-years remains debated (depending on measurement methods), and approximately 2600 light-years is adopted here.

mirfak.note: The brightest star in Perseus and a core member of the young open cluster Melotte 20; its luminosity is about 5000 times that of the Sun, and it is one of the brightest yellow-white supergiants visible to the naked eye.

hamal.note: The brightest star in Aries, with a mass only slightly larger than the Sun, yet its radius has expanded to about 15 times; the vernal equinox was near it more than two thousand years ago, hence the name 'Age of Aries'. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/lum_sun; Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

markab.note: A corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, a blue-white giant leaving the main sequence and evolving toward the red giant stage. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/radius_sun,physical/radius_km】

alpheratz.note: Historically classified as both Alpha Andromedae and Delta Pegasi, it is a shared corner of the two constellations; it is itself a spectroscopic binary, with the primary star hundreds of times brighter than the companion. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/orbital_period_years】

mirach.note: Jump two stations northeast from it to find the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a classic landmark for deep-sky observation; it is itself a spectroscopic binary.

wezen.note: The second-brightest star in Canis Major after Sirius; its diameter is about 188 times that of the Sun, yet its surface temperature is only a little more than half that of the Sun. It is a "puffy" supergiant and will end its life as a supernova.

adhara.note: It was closer to Earth about 4.7 million years ago and once became the brightest star in the whole sky at magnitude -3.99; today it remains the strongest extreme ultraviolet radiation source in the night sky, and its ultraviolet photons dominate the ionization state of the Local Interstellar Cloud. 【AI Review 2026-10-27 (Only 1 run succeeded): Empty:physical/lum_sun】

aludra.note: Together with Wezen and Aludra, it belongs to the Arabic "the Virgins" (al-Adhara) asterism; its mass is nearly 20 solar masses, luminosity exceeds 100,000 times that of the Sun, and it has reached the late stage of its life.

mu_cephei.note: Also known as the Garnet Star, famous for its garnet-like blood-red hue; its estimated radius ranges from 972~1650 R☉ depending on aperture, and 1260 R☉ is adopted here. Almost all of its ultraviolet light is absorbed by its own atmosphere.

uy_scuti.note: Once known for an old estimate of about 1708 R☉; latest observations revise its radius down to approximately 909 R☉ — still nearly one thousand times that of the Sun. Semiregular variable star, varying by about 1 magnitude over roughly 8.5 months.

rw_cephei.note: Semiregular variable star with a radius more than one thousand times the Sun's; in 2022 it underwent its deepest dimming on record, possibly linked to a large-scale dust ejection event.

s_persei.note: Red supergiant lying toward the Perseus Double Cluster, with a mass of roughly 20 M☉ and radius of about 1200 R☉; its brightness variation is close to 1 magnitude, making it the 'hidden giant' in the Double Cluster observing field.

mira.note: Its magnitude fluctuates between 2 mag and 10 mag with a period of approximately 332 days: visible to the naked eye at maximum brightness, requiring a telescope at minimum. It is losing mass vigorously, trailing a roughly 13-light-year-long tail in its stellar wind.

p_cygni.note: Suddenly brightened to 3rd magnitude in 1600, then faded slowly; it still ejects material via a powerful stellar wind. Similar to Eta Carinae, it is the prototype of the "false supernova" phenomenon.

naos.note: Surface temperature ~42000 K, one of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye; luminosity ~500,000 times that of the Sun, stellar wind speed up to ~2200 km/s. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/mass_sun,physical/mass_kg,physical/lum_sun; Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

r136a1.note: Currently the most massive known star (~291 M☉, near the theoretical upper limit of stellar mass), luminosity ~7.24 million times that of the Sun; its powerful stellar wind sheds mass equivalent to several Earths each year. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/lum_sun】

algol.note: Every 2.87 days, the fainter companion passes in front of the primary star, brightness plummets from magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 and lasts ~10 hours — a cosmic "blink"; it was named the "Demon Star" in ancient China for this reason. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/lum_sun; Fill:orbit/semimajor_axis_au,orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/inclination_deg】

sheliak.note: The two stars are so close that material flows from one to the other, enveloped by a common envelope; light variation is nearly continuous, and it is one of the earliest confirmed eclipsing binaries. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:physical/mass_sun; Fill:orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/inclination_deg,orbit/eccentricity,orbit/rotation_period_hours】

almaaz.subtype: Eclipsing variable star (F0Iab primary + dust disk companion)
almaaz.note: A rare stellar eclipse lasting about 2 years occurs every 27.1 years; the occulting body is thought to be a companion wrapped in a massive dust disk. Estimates for the primary mass diverge widely (roughly 2.2~15 M☉), with no consensus, so mass is left blank honestly. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Leave blank:distance_ly; Fill:physical/mass_sun,physical/mass_kg,orbit/orbital_period_years,orbit/inclination_deg,orbit/eccentricity】

kepler_452.note: Hosts exoplanet Kepler-452b: the first confirmed planet with an Earth-like radius located in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star, with an orbital period of about 385 days, nicknamed 'Earth's cousin'. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Leave blank:distance_ly】

kepler_22.note: Hosts Kepler-22b: the first confirmed exoplanet located in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star, with a radius roughly 2.4 times Earth's, and may be an 'ocean world'. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

trappist_1.note: An ultracool red dwarf only slightly larger than Jupiter, yet it hosts 7 Earth-sized planets; 3~4 of them lie in the habitable zone. All planets are tightly packed, appearing as large 'moons' in the sky when viewed from the innermost world. JWST is searching its atmospheres for signs of life.

gliese_581.note: A red dwarf merely 20.4 light-years from Earth with multiple confirmed exoplanets. Whether Gliese 581g/c/d are habitable sparked long-running debates, marking one of the most famous early episodes in exoplanet science. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

kepler_186.note: It has five planets; the outermost one, Kepler-186f, is the first confirmed exoplanet within the habitable zone with a radius close to Earth. However, its sunlight is far dimmer than Earth’s, and noon there may resemble dusk on Earth.

cancri_55.note: A binary system with five discovered exoplanets; 55 Cancri e is a famous 'super-Earth' whose surface temperature is high enough to melt rock, possibly forming a magma ocean.

pegasi_51.note: The first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like star (51 Pegasi b, a 'hot Jupiter') was found here; the two discoverers were awarded the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics, marking the start of the exoplanet era.

beta_pictoris.note: It hosts the first stellar debris disk imaged directly, with two confirmed giant planets (Beta Pictoris b/c) in the disk. It is also the namesake of the 'Beta Pictoris moving group', a group of young stars only about 20 million years old. 【AI Reviewed 2026-10-27：Fill:orbit/rotation_period_hours】

procyon_a.note: Procyon B is a white dwarf with a mass of approximately 0.6 solar masses and a radius roughly equal to Earth's. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Clear:physical/radius_sun,physical/radius_km】
procyon_a.members: Binary system composed of Procyon A (primary star) and Procyon B (white dwarf companion)

orcus.note: Diameter approximately 910 km (range 870–960 km); mass equals the total mass of the Orcus+Vanth binary system, with Orcus itself accounting for about 90%; in 3:2 orbital resonance with Neptune, belonging to the plutino group. 【AI Review 2026-10-27：Clear:physical/mass_sun,orbit/rotation_period_hours】

vanth.note: Diameter approximately 440 km; mass roughly 1/20 of Orcus, density and albedo are approximate estimates. The two bodies orbit each other in nearly circular orbits and are mutually tidally locked, forming a 2:3 Neptune-resonant plutino binary system.

gonggong_225088.note: Diameter ~1230 km (radius 615 km); mass adopted as 1.75×10^21 kg, with a range of 1.75~2.25×10^21 kg from different observations; early measurement of rotation period was 22.4 h, later HST observations revised it to ~22.4 h or 44.8 h (caused by suspected bimodal albedo), 22.4 h is adopted here; surface temperature ~30 K, albedo ~0.1~0.15; distance calculated from semi-major axis 67.5 AU. 【AI Review 2026-10-27 (only 1 run succeeded): Clear:distance_ly,physical/mass_sun,physical/mass_kg; Fill:orbit/orbital_velocity_km_s】
gonggong_225088.members: Has 1 known satellite: Xiangliu (Xiangliu, diameter ~100 km)

pallas.note: Pallas is the second-largest asteroid in the Solar System (second only to Ceres by volume and mass), but due to its highly irregular shape (similar to a flattened potato), its equivalent radius is approximately 512 km. Its orbital inclination reaches 34.8 degrees, much larger than other large asteroids. 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Clear:orbit/obliquity_deg,orbit/rotation_period_hours】

hygiea.note: Mass and radius are approximate observational values; whether it is a dwarf planet remains controversial 【2 runs inconsistent:orbit/rotation_period_hours(13.83 vs 27.6), pending manual verification】 【AI Review 2026-10-27: Fill:orbit/obliquity_deg】
